claim: Deletion of mitochondrial DNA in eukaryotes is currently attributed to rare accidental events associated with mitochondrial replication or repair of double-strand breaks.
source: Deletion of mitochondrial DNA in eukaryotes is currently attributed to rare accidental events associated with mitochondrial replication or repair of double-strand breaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nissanka et al., 2019, which provides scholarly support for the current understanding of mtDNA deletion mechanisms.

claim: Yeast cells arrest harmful intramitochondrial superoxide production by shutting down respiration through genetically controlled deletion of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation genes.
source: We report the discovery that yeast cells arrest harmful intramitochondrial superoxide production by shutting down respiration through genetically controlled deletion of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation genes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript including adaptation experiments, mtDNA sequencing, and deletion strain experiments.

claim: The mtDNA deletion process critically involves the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 2.
source: We show that this process critically involves the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 2 and two-way mitochondrial-nuclear communication through Rtg2 and Rtg3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that sod2Δ populations fail to adapt to paraquat and do not show mtDNA deletions, as presented in Figure 4.

claim: The mtDNA deletion process critically involves two-way mitochondrial-nuclear communication through Rtg2 and Rtg3.
source: We show that this process critically involves the antioxidant enzyme superoxide dismutase 2 and two-way mitochondrial-nuclear communication through Rtg2 and Rtg3.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ populations fail to adapt to paraquat, as presented in Figure 5.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA homeostasis is rapidly restored after cessation of a short-term superoxide stress.
source: While mitochondrial DNA homeostasis is rapidly restored after cessation of a short-term superoxide stress, long-term stress causes maladaptive persistence of the deletion process, leading to complete annihilation of the cellular pool of intact mitochondrial genomes and irrevocable loss of respiratory ability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rapid restoration of mtDNA and respiratory growth after release from short-term paraquat exposure, as shown in Figures 3D and 6A.

claim: Long-term superoxide stress causes maladaptive persistence of the deletion process, leading to complete annihilation of the cellular pool of intact mitochondrial genomes and irrevocable loss of respiratory ability.
source: While mitochondrial DNA homeostasis is rapidly restored after cessation of a short-term superoxide stress, long-term stress causes maladaptive persistence of the deletion process, leading to complete annihilation of the cellular pool of intact mitochondrial genomes and irrevocable loss of respiratory ability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that after extended paraquat exposure, populations lose their capacity to restore respiratory growth and retain only small mtDNA segments, as shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mitochondrial impairment is strongly associated with aging.
source: Mitochondrial impairment is strongly associated with aging (Sun et al., 2016) and the pathogenesis of age-related human diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (Hu et al., 2017), Parkinson's disease (Ammal Kaidery and Thomas, 2018), the deterioration of skeletal and cardiac muscle (Hepple, 2016), and macular degeneration (Hyttinen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature (Sun et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2017; Ammal Kaidery and Thomas, 2018; Hepple, 2016; Hyttinen et al., 2018).

claim: Mitochondrial DNA deletions are perceived to contribute markedly to age-related mitochondrial impairment.
source: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) deletions are perceived to contribute markedly to this impairment (Krishnan et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krishnan et al., 2008.

claim: mtDNA deletions are prone to cripple oxidative phosphorylation.
source: However, considering that mtDNA deletions are prone to cripple oxidative phosphorylation (Fontana and Gahlon, 2020) (OXPHOS), and thus turn off the production of intramitochondrial superoxide anion (O2∙−), it is conceivable that mtDNA deletion is also under genetic control.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fontana and Gahlon, 2020.

claim: Domestication has systematically enhanced fermentative and reduced respiratory asexual growth in yeast.
source: Domestication has systematically enhanced fermentative and reduced respiratory asexual growth (De Chiara et al., 2020), with common lab strains harboring multiple defects in mitochondrial respiratory biology (Gaisne et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Chiara et al., 2020 and Gaisne et al., 1999.

claim: Common lab strains harbor multiple defects in mitochondrial respiratory biology.
source: Domestication has systematically enhanced fermentative and reduced respiratory asexual growth (De Chiara et al., 2020), with common lab strains harboring multiple defects in mitochondrial respiratory biology (Gaisne et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gaisne et al., 1999.

claim: Paraquat generates O2∙− by passing electrons from OXPHOS complex III and mitochondrial NADPH dehydrogenases to O2.
source: Paraquat generates O2∙− by passing electrons from OXPHOS complex III and mitochondrial NADPH dehydrogenases to O2 (Cochemé and Murphy, 2008; Castello et al., 2007), a mode of O2∙− generation that is a good proxy for the in vivo situation (Zou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cochemé and Murphy, 2008 and Castello et al., 2007.

claim: Paraquat exposure at 400 µg/mL causes a 2.5-3 fold increase in cell doubling time.
source: We titrated the paraquat dose to cause a 2.5-3 fold increase in cell doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 400 µg/mL paraquat, key mitochondrial oxidative stress response genes (Sod1, Sod2, and Ccp1) increased their transcript levels 2–12-fold in early lag-phase.
source: At the chosen concentration (400 µg/mL), key mitochondrial oxidative stress response genes, copper/zinc dependent O2∙− dismutase (Cu/ZnSOD, Sod1), manganese-dependent O2∙− dismutase (MnSOD, Sod2) and mitochondrial cytochrome C peroxidase (Ccp1), increased their transcript levels 2–12-fold in early lag-phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of vitamin C caused the growth of paraquat exposed wild type cells to be on par with that of unexposed wild type cells.
source: Addition of vitamin C, an antioxidant that accepts electrons from PQ+, the free radical (or 'damaging') state of paraquat (Sendra et al., 1999), caused the growth of paraquat exposed wild type cells, as well as paraquat exposed sod2Δ cells, to be on par with that of unexposed wild type cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: A paraquat concentration of 400 µg/mL impaired cell growth entirely through its effect on O2∙− production.
source: This suggested that a paraquat concentration of 400 µg/mL impaired cell growth entirely through its effect on O2∙− production.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the vitamin C rescue experiment data showing that vitamin C, which counters paraquat-induced O2∙− production, fully restores growth.

claim: All 96 cell populations exposed to paraquat adapted much faster than every other cell population exposed to any other stressor.
source: All 96 cell populations exposed to paraquat adapted much faster than every other cell population exposed to any other stressor (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative adaptation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Between 4 and 10 cell generations, paraquat-exposed populations on average reduced their doubling time by 106 min, corresponding to 49.3% of the maximum possible reduction.
source: Between 4 and 10 cell generations, populations on average reduced their doubling time by 106 min. Assuming the minimum achievable cell doubling time to be that of the wild type before exposure to paraquat (a mean of 93 min), this corresponded to 49.3% of the maximum possible reduction.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of the adaptation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: After the initial swift adaptation phase, adaptation entered a second phase where the reduction in cell doubling time progressed much slower until it plateaued after 75 generations at 72.6% of the maximum possible reduction.
source: Thenceforth, adaptation entered a second phase where the reduction in cell doubling time progressed much slower until it plateaued after 75 generations at 72.6% of the maximum possible reduction (mean) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the temporal adaptation data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A numerical model combining population genetics and population dynamics theory with existing data on yeast mutation rates was unable to reproduce the observed extraordinarily swift response to paraquat.
source: The numerical model was completely unable to reproduce the observed extraordinarily swift response to paraquat, indicating that nuclear mutations were unlikely to explain the phenomenon (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All 96 paraquat-adapted cell populations retained their acquired tolerance to paraquat for only 1–3 growth cycles before abruptly losing it after release from stress.
source: All 96 cell populations retained their acquired tolerance to paraquat (mean reduction in cell doubling time: 106 min) for only 1–3 growth cycles before abruptly losing it (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress-release experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Populations adapted to arsenic and glycine lost their acquired adaptations more slowly and gradually than paraquat-adapted populations.
source: When employing the same experimental procedure to 96 cell populations from each of the two other environments to which adaptation was also fast (arsenic and glycine), we found that despite the presence of a much stronger Darwinian counterselection (Figure 1C), these populations lost their acquired adaptations more slowly and gradually (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative stress-release experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Paraquat caused a rapid shift (<5 hr) from a tubular to a fragmented mitochondrial organization.
source: We therefore first assayed mitochondrial morphology before, during and after paraquat exposure by confocal and electron microscopy. In both cases, paraquat caused a rapid shift (<5 hr) from a tubular to a fragmented mitochondrial organization (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal and electron microscopy data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: After removing the paraquat stress, mitochondrial organization rapidly reversed (<5 hr) back to a tubular organization.
source: After removing the paraquat stress we observed a rapid reversal (<5 hr) back to a tubular organization (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cumulative mitochondrial volume remained near pre-stress levels with at the most a marginal reduction after 77–79 hr of paraquat exposure.
source: Nevertheless, the cumulative mitochondrial volume remained near pre-stress levels with at the most a marginal reduction after 77–79 hr of paraquat exposure (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative microscopy data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Cell populations lacking Atg32 adapted to paraquat over ~80 generations as wild-type populations.
source: Most importantly, cell populations (n=16) lacking Atg32, a key component of canonical mitophagy (Liu and Okamoto, 2021), adapted to paraquat over ~80 generations as wild-type populations (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental adaptation data for atg32Δ strains shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The initial swift adaptation to paraquat did not depend on canonical mitophagy.
source: This led us to conclude that the initial swift adaptation to paraquat did not depend on canonical mitophagy.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental data showing that atg32Δ populations adapt as well as wild-type populations.

claim: In all five sequenced populations, the mean mtDNA copy number decreased dramatically during the early phase of paraquat adaptation.
source: We first used short read sequencing to measure the mean coverage of the mitochondrial genome in five of the 96 yeast cell populations adapting to paraquat (Figure 3A). In all five populations, we found the mean mtDNA copy number to decrease dramatically during the early phase of paraquat adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All nine qPCR-tracked cell populations lost copy numbers of some, but not all, mtDNA-encoded genes during the early adaptation phase.
source: This led us to use qPCR to track changes in the copy numbers of individual mtDNA genes in nine paraquat-adapting cell populations. We found that all nine cell populations lost copy numbers of some, but not all, mtDNA-encoded genes during the early adaptation phase (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adjacent mtDNA genes were lost concomitantly and to the same extent, implying deletion of entire mtDNA segments.
source: As adjacent genes were lost concomitantly, and to the same extent, the observed loss in copy numbers implied that the early adaptation phase was associated with deletion of entire mtDNA segments.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the qPCR data showing coordinated loss of adjacent genes.

claim: All nine cell populations lost one or more segments within the mtDNA region spanning COX1 to VAR1.
source: In addition, the qPCR data showed that the lost segments were unevenly distributed across the mitochondrial genome: all nine cell populations lost one or more segments within the mtDNA region spanning COX1 to VAR1, while a few also lost the 21 S rRNA and COX2 rapidly thereafter.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing consistent deletion patterns across populations.

claim: The retained mtDNA segments, which in all nine cases encompassed COX3-RPM1 and 15 S rRNA, remained at near founder level throughout the early adaptation phase.
source: The retained mtDNA segments, which in all nine cases encompassed COX3-RPM1 and 15 S rRNA, remained at near founder lever throughout the early adaptation phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing stable copy numbers for specific mtDNA regions.

claim: The mtDNA coverage prior to paraquat adaptation was perfectly even.
source: Since the mtDNA coverage prior to paraquat adaptation was perfectly even (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), the observed mtDNA loss was clearly induced by paraquat.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The early paraquat adaptation coincided almost perfectly with loss of respiratory growth.
source: We therefore tested the respiratory growth capacity of the adapted populations by growing them on glycerol and found that the early paraquat adaptation coincided almost perfectly with loss of respiratory growth (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by respiratory growth assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The rapid loss of the acquired adaptations after removal of the O2∙− stress coincided with the restoration of the capacity for respiratory growth.
source: Similarly, the rapid loss of the acquired adaptations after removal of the O2∙− stress coincided with the restoration of the capacity for respiratory growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress-release experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The five populations quickly restored their capacity for respiratory growth after removal of paraquat, and this restoration coincided with the reestablishment of the wild type mtDNA profile and the loss of the acquired paraquat adaptation.
source: As expected, the five populations quickly restored their capacity for respiratory growth after removal of paraquat, and this restoration coincided with the reestablishment of the wild type mtDNA profile and the loss of the acquired paraquat adaptation (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated data from respiratory growth assays and DNA sequencing shown in Figures 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: ρ0 yeast cells devoid of mtDNA and OXPHOS growing on a normal glucose medium show a twofold decrease in cellular O2∙− production.
source: Together with the observation that ρ0 yeast cells devoid of mtDNA devoid of OXPHOS growing on a normal glucose medium show a twofold decrease in cellular O2∙− production (Reddi and Culotta, 2013), the data led us to hypothesize that the reduction of paraquat toxicity, leading to a substantial reduction in cell doubling time during the first adaptation phase, was closely associated with the loss of OXPHOS caused by loss of critical mtDNA segments.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Reddi and Culotta, 2013.

claim: mip1Δ cells were preadapted to paraquat as their growth was equivalent to that of wild-type populations after these had undergone nine generations of adaptation to paraquat.
source: The mip1Δ cells were clearly preadapted to paraquat as their growth was equivalent to that of wild-type populations after these had undergone nine generations of adaptation to paraquat (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative growth data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The adaptation rate of mip1Δ populations exposed to paraquat was on par with the adaptation rate of wild-type cells in their second phase of adaptation.
source: Together with the finding that the adaptation rate of mip1Δ populations exposed to paraquat was on par with the adaptation rate of wild-type cells in their second phase of adaptation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A), this implies that loss of OXPHOS due to loss of mtDNA segments was indeed the most important factor underlying the first adaptation phase (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative adaptation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Genes encoding mitochondrial proteins were overrepresented in the 100 most paraquat-resistant deletion strains (32.3% vs 18.6%, permutation test, p=0.00314).
source: Genes encoding mitochondrial proteins were overrepresented in the 100 most paraquat-resistant deletion strains (32.3% vs 18.6%, permutation test, p=0.00314).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the yeast deletion collection screen data.

claim: Gene deletion strains with low mtDNA copy number convert a cell doubling time defect in absence of paraquat into a cell doubling time advantage in presence of paraquat.
source: As a group, these strains convert a cell doubling time defect in absence of paraquat (mean 16 min slower than deletion strains with a normal mtDNA copy number of 5–35 copies, p=3.05*10–6) into a cell doubling time advantage in presence of paraquat (mean 13 min faster than deletion strains with a normal mtDNA copy number of 5–35 copies, p=0.045).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of growth data from the yeast deletion collection.

claim: Paraquat adapted cells were strongly preadapted to menadione, and this preadaptation became manifest during the early paraquat adaptation, concomitant with the mtDNA loss.
source: However, they were strongly preadapted to menadione, and this preadaptation became manifest during the early paraquat adaptation, that is concomitant with the mtDNA loss (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-resistance experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Cells lacking either Sod1 or Sod2 showed virtually no growth when exposed to 400 μg/mL paraquat.
source: Cells lacking either one of the O2∙− dismutases showed virtually no growth when exposed to the original paraquat dose (400 μg/mL) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating the importance of enzymatic O2∙− dismutation.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data for sod1Δ and sod2Δ strains shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 12.5 μg/mL paraquat, sod1Δ populations adapted as the wild-type populations, while sod2Δ populations barely showed any adaptive response.
source: At this concentration, we found that the sod1Δ populations, in terms of reduction in cell doubling time, adapted as the wild-type populations over 10 growth cycles, while the sod2Δ populations barely showed any adaptive response (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative adaptation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Four out of eight sod2Δ populations exposed to 50 μg/mL paraquat showed very marginal adaptation and their mtDNA gene copy number remained at, or near, pre-stress levels.
source: Four populations still showed very marginal adaptation and we confirmed by qPCR that their mtDNA gene copy number remained at, or near, pre-stress levels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The remaining four sod2Δ populations exposed to 50 μg/mL paraquat had a very delayed adaptation that coincided with different, single mtDNA deletions.
source: The remaining four populations had a very delayed adaptation that coincided with different, single mtDNA deletions (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by adaptation and qPCR data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In 50 μg/mL of paraquat there was a marked reduction in doubling time in sod2Δmip1Δ populations relative to sod2Δ populations, similar to the difference between mip1Δ populations and wild type populations in 400 μg/mL of paraquat.
source: In 50 μg/mL of paraquat there was a marked reduction in doubling time in sod2Δmip1Δ populations relative to sod2Δ populations. The difference was similar to the one between mip1Δ populations and wild type populations in 400 μg/mL of paraquat (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative growth data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The delayed adaptation in sod2Δ strains was because the mtDNA deletions causing shutdown of OXPHOS emerged at a much lower rate than in the wild type.
source: This implies that the delayed adaptation in sod2Δ strains was because the mtDNA deletions causing shutdown of OXPHOS emerged at a much lower rate than in the wild type.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparative data on sod2Δ, sod2Δmip1Δ, and wild-type populations.

claim: The location of the redox signaling involved in the triggering of the mtDNA deletion response is the mitochondrial matrix.
source: While Sod2 is located in the mitochondrial matrix, Sod1 is located in the cytosol and mitochondrial intermembrane space. The fact that sod1Δ populations adapted as the wild type suggests that the location of the redox signaling involved in the triggering of the mtDNA deletion response is the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential adaptation of sod1Δ and sod2Δ populations combined with knowledge of the subcellular localization of these proteins.

claim: Without Sod2 the cells appear incapable of launching the speedy mtDNA deletion process observed in the wild type.
source: Regardless of which signals and processes within the matrix that are responsible for inducing and propagating down-stream effects, the above results strongly suggest that without Sod2 the cells appear incapable of launching the speedy mtDNA deletion process we observe in the wild type.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing lack of adaptation and mtDNA deletion in sod2Δ populations.

claim: Deletion of mtDNA alters the expression of a multitude of genes resulting in increased glycolytic production of ATP, dubbed the retrograde response.
source: In budding yeast, deletion of mtDNA alters the expression of a multitude of genes resulting in increased glycolytic production of ATP (Epstein et al., 2001), dubbed the retrograde response.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Epstein et al., 2001.

claim: Upon mitochondrial OXPHOS dysfunction, the cytosolic protein Rtg2 causes the transcription factors Rtg1 and Rtg3 to translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus where they together activate retrograde transcription.
source: Upon mitochondrial OXPHOS dysfunction, the cytosolic protein Rtg2 (Sekito et al., 2000) causes the transcription factors Rtg1 and Rtg3 to translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus where they together activate retrograde transcription (Rothermel et al., 1995; Rothermel et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sekito et al., 2000; Rothermel et al., 1995; and Rothermel et al., 1997.

claim: Activation of retrograde transcription has been reported to cause mtDNA deletions.
source: However, activation of retrograde transcription has also been reported to cause mtDNA deletions (Farooq et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Farooq et al., 2013.

claim: All rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ cell populations failed to adapt to paraquat over 80 generations.
source: We therefore probed whether the retrograde response is required for paraquat-induced mtDNA deletions by exposing rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ cell populations (n=16) to paraquat for 80 generations. In both cases, all cell populations failed to adapt (Figure 5A), and their capacity for respiratory growth was virtually unperturbed at the end of the experiment (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by adaptation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The capacity for respiratory growth was virtually unperturbed in rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ populations after 70–78 generations of paraquat adaptation.
source: We therefore probed whether the retrograde response is required for paraquat-induced mtDNA deletions by exposing rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ cell populations (n=16) to paraquat for 80 generations. In both cases, all cell populations failed to adapt (Figure 5A), and their capacity for respiratory growth was virtually unperturbed at the end of the experiment (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by respiratory growth data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The growth of the rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ populations was similar to that of the wild type in the presence as well as the absence of paraquat.
source: Importantly, the growth of the rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ populations was similar to that of the wild type in the presence as well as the absence of paraquat.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative growth data for these strains.

claim: The data strongly support the notions that the mtDNA deletion process is under regulatory control and that this regulation is dependent on a two-way mito-nuclear communication facilitated by Rtg2 and Rtg3.
source: Thus, the data strongly support the notions that the mtDNA deletion process is under regulatory control and that this regulation is dependent on a two-way mito-nuclear communication facilitated by Rtg2 and Rtg3.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that rtg2Δ and rtg3Δ populations fail to undergo mtDNA deletion and adaptation.

claim: 44 of the 96 populations had completely lost their capacity for restoring the pool of intact mtDNA genomes back to pre-stress levels after 24 generations of paraquat exposure.
source: We found that 44 of the 96 populations had completely lost their capacity for restoring the pool of intact mtDNA genomes back to pre-stress levels after 24 generations of paraquat exposure, and after 242 generations all did (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress-release experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: After 242 generations of paraquat exposure, all populations had completely lost their capacity for restoring the pool of intact mtDNA genomes back to pre-stress levels.
source: We found that 44 of the 96 populations had completely lost their capacity for restoring the pool of intact mtDNA genomes back to pre-stress levels after 24 generations of paraquat exposure, and after 242 generations all did (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress-release experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the five sequenced cell populations, the capacity to restore the copy numbers of intact mtDNA and the respiratory growth after removal of stress was lost between 15 and 42 generations of paraquat exposure.
source: Moreover, in the five sequenced cell populations, the capacity to restore the copy numbers of intact mtDNA and the respiratory growth after removal of stress was lost between 15 and 42 generations of paraquat exposure (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated data from sequencing and respiratory growth assays shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Out of 44 sequenced endpoint populations, 25 populations had almost completely lost their entire 77 kb mtDNA (97–99%), retaining only small (<1 kb) segments.
source: We therefore assayed the mtDNA loss in 44 sequenced endpoint (t50) populations. Out of these, 25 populations had almost completely lost their entire 77 kb mtDNA (97–99%), retaining only small (<1 kb) segments (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B), in line with previous reports (Fangman et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: 18 endpoint populations remained in a rho negative (ρ-) state, retaining 6–34 kb mtDNA segments with copy numbers somewhat above the original founder levels (mean: 20% increase).
source: 18 endpoint populations remained in a rho negative (ρ-) state, retaining 6–34 kb mtDNA segments with copy numbers somewhat above the original founder levels (mean: 20% increase).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA sequencing data from endpoint populations.

claim: The mtDNA genes in the region spanning COX1 to VAR1 were lost in all, or almost all, 18 ρ- endpoint populations.
source: The mtDNA genes in the region spanning COX1 to VAR1 were lost in all, or almost all, 18 populations, while COX3-RPM1 and 15 S rRNA were retained in most populations, confirming the deletion bias observed in the early adaptation phase (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: COX3-RPM1 and 15 S rRNA were retained in most ρ- endpoint populations.
source: The mtDNA genes in the region spanning COX1 to VAR1 were lost in all, or almost all, 18 populations, while COX3-RPM1 and 15 S rRNA were retained in most populations, confirming the deletion bias observed in the early adaptation phase (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The coverage across the retained mtDNA segments was even in each of the 18 ρ- endpoint populations, most likely reflecting a single continuous stretch of mtDNA.
source: The coverage across the retained mtDNA segments was even in each of these 18 ρ- endpoint populations, the most likely explanation being that it reflected a single continuous stretch of mtDNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is inferred from DNA sequencing coverage data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Nanopore sequencing confirmed that many reads spanned the entire set of retained segments in endpoint populations D1 and A7.
source: To confirm this, we sequenced two end point populations (D1 and A7) with longer Nanopore reads. As expected, we found that many reads spanned the entire set of retained segments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-read sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Some retained mtDNA segments persisted as linear tandem amplifications.
source: The alignment data also suggested that some retained mtDNA segments persisted as linear tandem amplifications. To confirm this, we performed a PCR directed outwards across the ends of the retained mtDNA segments. This would produce a product only if two copies of the mtDNA segments were located next to each other on the same mtDNA molecule (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C). The PCR resulted in the expected product in the D1 endpoint population, showing that at least some of the mtDNA molecules in this population must therefore have been tandemly amplified, in line with the standard configuration of intact mtDNA in yeast cells (Maleszka et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The ρ-- populations (those that lost almost all mtDNA) grew slower on paraquat than the ρ- populations (those retaining 6-34 kb segments).
source: To assess whether there was an adaptive advantage associated with the sustained depletion of mtDNA, we compared the doubling times of the ρ- populations still retaining 6–34 kb mtDNA segments with those that had lost almost all their mtDNA. Intriguingly, the latter group consistently grew slower on paraquat than the former (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative growth data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The sustained mtDNA depletion under long-term stress, leading to irreversible loss of intact mtDNA genomes, is an artifactual response driven by prolonged induction of a regulatory mechanism dimensioned by natural selection to handle O2∙− stress it can successfully deal with before the pool of intact mtDNA genomes disappears.
source: This suggests that the sustained mtDNA depletion under long-term stress, leading to irreversible loss of intact mtDNA genomes, is an artifactual response driven by prolonged induction of a regulatory mechanism dimensioned by natural selection to handle O2∙− stress it can successfully deal with before the pool of intact mtDNA genomes disappears.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that complete mtDNA loss is maladaptive compared to partial retention.

claim: All but four endpoint populations carried extra copies of chromosomes II (n=29), III (n=21) and/or V (n=16) at near fixation (mean p: 0.97).
source: However, all but four endpoint populations carried extra copies of chromosomes II (n=29), III (n=21) and/or V (n=16) (Figure 6—figure supplement 5A) at near fixation (mean p: 0.97).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5A.

claim: In the five sequenced populations with time-resolved data, chromosome gains appeared after the early and very swift O2∙− adaptation phase.
source: In the five sequenced populations for which we had time-resolved data, these chromosome gains appeared after the early and very swift O2∙− adaptation phase (Figure 6—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-resolved sequencing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Part of the paraquat resistance and part of the loss of respiratory growth co-segregated with chromosomes II and V aneuploidies.
source: To assess their contribution to the second phase of adaptation, we crossed clones carrying the individual aneuploidies back to wild type cells over three consecutive meiotic generations. We then compared the tolerance for paraquat, and the capacity for respiratory growth, in offspring with and without extra chromosomes. Part of the paraquat resistance and part of the loss of respiratory growth co-segregated with chromosomes II and V aneuploidies.
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic segregation analysis data.

claim: The duplications of chromosome II and V caused a reduction in respiratory growth relative to the wild type (cell doubling times: 5.7 hr (chr II), 4.9 hr (chr V), 3.3 hr (WT)).
source: The duplications of chromosome II and V caused a reduction in respiratory growth relative to the wild type (cell doubling times: 5.7 hr (chr II), 4.9 hr (chr V), 3.3 hr (WT)) (Figure 6—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by respiratory growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Duplication of chromosome II reduced the cell doubling time during paraquat exposure by 31 min.
source: They also reduced the cell doubling time during paraquat exposure by 31 and 38 min, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5D.

claim: Duplication of chromosome V reduced the cell doubling time during paraquat exposure by 38 min.
source: They also reduced the cell doubling time during paraquat exposure by 31 and 38 min, respectively (Figure 6—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5D.

claim: Duplication of chromosome III caused no apparent reduction in cell doubling time.
source: Duplication of chromosome III caused no apparent reduction in cell doubling time.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth data from the chromosome duplication segregation analysis.

claim: Assuming an additive phenotypic effect of the chromosome II and V duplications, the cell doubling time would be reduced by 69 min, which together with the effect from the mtDNA deletions would correspond to cells realizing 81% of the possible adaptation.
source: Assuming an additive phenotypic effect of the chromosome II and V duplications, the cell doubling time would be reduced by 69 min. Together with the effect from the mtDNA deletions disrupting OXPHOS function, this would correspond to cells realizing 81% of the possible adaptation. As the cells actually realized on average 72.6%, an approximately additive phenotypic effect of these duplications appears to fully explain the second phase of adaptation in populations having both duplications genetically fixed.
evidence: This claim is inferred from quantitative analysis of the combined effects of mtDNA deletions and chromosome duplications.

claim: The lack of adaptation of the sod2Δ, rtg2Δ, and rtg3Δ populations are hard to reconcile with the operation of random O2∙− induced mtDNA deletions and subsequent selection of cells possessing OXPHOS-impaired mitochondria.
source: As argued above, the lack of adaptation of the sod2Δ, rtg2Δ, and rtg3Δ populations are hard to reconcile with the operation of random O2∙− induced mtDNA deletions (e.g. caused by genomic instability) and subsequent selection of cells possessing OXPHOS-impaired mitochondria.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that deletion of specific genes prevents adaptation.

claim: The data support the notion that the observed deletion of mtDNA segments causing loss of OXPHOS activity is under regulatory control.
source: Instead, the data support the notion that the observed deletion of mtDNA segments causing loss of OXPHOS activity is under regulatory control.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental evidence showing dependence on specific regulatory proteins.

claim: It is apt to denote the regulatory process of mtDNA deletion as 'mtDNA editing' as it alters the mtDNA content to suit a particular purpose.
source: We think it is apt to denote this regulatory process as 'mtDNA editing' as it alters the mtDNA content to suit a particular purpose (Merriam-Webster's Coll Thes, 2021).
evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the interpretation of the experimental data and the definition of 'editing'.

claim: There was a clear preference for deletions within the COX1-VAR1 region during the first adaptation phase.
source: However, the fidelity of the mtDNA deletion mechanism in terms of which mtDNA segments are lost in the first adaptation phase does seem to be moderate. Still, there was a clear preference for deletions within the COX1-VAR1 region, and the segment containing COX3, RPM1, and 15 S RNA were not deleted in this phase, and more rarely also in the second adaptation phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and sequencing data showing consistent deletion patterns across populations.

claim: The segment containing COX3, RPM1, and 15 S RNA were not deleted in the first adaptation phase, and more rarely also in the second adaptation phase.
source: However, the fidelity of the mtDNA deletion mechanism in terms of which mtDNA segments are lost in the first adaptation phase does seem to be moderate. Still, there was a clear preference for deletions within the COX1-VAR1 region, and the segment containing COX3, RPM1, and 15 S RNA were not deleted in this phase, and more rarely also in the second adaptation phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and sequencing data showing retention of specific mtDNA regions.

claim: All paraquat adapting cell populations lost either COB itself, or genes required for COB expression, during the first adaptation phase.
source: But it should be noted that all our paraquat adapting cell populations lost either COB itself, or genes required for COB expression, during the first adaptation phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR and sequencing data from all analyzed populations.

claim: The speedy restoration of the wild type mtDNA pool after release from paraquat is most probably due to proliferation of heteroplasmic cells that become homoplasmic through recovery of their wild type mtDNA profile.
source: The speedy restoration of the wild type mtDNA pool after release from paraquat is most probably due to proliferation of heteroplasmic cells that become homoplasmic through recovery of their wild type mtDNA profile.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the observed rapid restoration of mtDNA.

claim: The lack of selective advantage for the wild type mtDNA implies that recovery is not caused by a Darwinian process based on differences in cell doubling time.
source: However, the lack of selective advantage for the wild type mtDNA (Figure 1B and C) implies that this recovery is not caused by a Darwinian process based on differences in cell doubling time.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the stress-release experimental data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Either the replication of the mtDNA genomes possessing deletions has to stop, or the standing pool of these mtDNA genomes specifically has to be removed by some sort of targeted mitophagy, or both processes may be simultaneously operative.
source: Thus, either the replication of the mtDNA genomes possessing deletions has to stop (Jakubke et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020), or the standing pool of these mtDNA genomes specifically has to be removed by some sort of targeted mitophagy (Twig et al., 2008; Ban et al., 2017) . Both processes may also be simultaneously operative.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: If the results extend to human cells, the results may prove to be of etiological as well as therapeutic importance with regard to age-related mitochondrial impairment and disease.
source: If the results extend to human cells, the results may prove to be of etiological as well as therapeutic importance with regard to age-related mitochondrial impairment and disease.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential implications if the findings are conserved in humans.

claim: Budding yeast and humans share a range of evolutionary conserved mechanisms concerning respiratory chain biology and mitochondrial quality control, including antioxidant enzymes and key proteins regulating mitophagy.
source: Budding yeast and humans share a range of evolutionary conserved mechanisms concerning respiratory chain biology and mitochondrial quality control, including antioxidant enzymes and key proteins regulating mitophagy (Montava-Garriga and Ganley, 2020; Kumar and Reichert, 2021; Barrientos, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Montava-Garriga and Ganley, 2020; Kumar and Reichert, 2021; and Barrientos, 2003.

claim: Doxorubicin and cisplatin both accumulate in mitochondria, where they induce O2∙− production through redox cycling.
source: In light of this, the available data on the cancer therapeutics doxorubicin and cisplatin suggest that our main results may extend to post-mitotic cells. They both accumulate in mitochondria (Kalyanaraman et al., 2002; Genc et al., 2014), where they induce O2∙− production through redox cycling (Malhi et al., 2012; Song et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kalyanaraman et al., 2002; Genc et al., 2014; Malhi et al., 2012; and Song et al., 2017.

claim: Long-term administration of doxorubicin and cisplatin cause oxidative injury to a variety of cells and tissues.
source: Their long-term administration cause oxidative injury to a variety of cells and tissues (Song et al., 2017; Songbo et al., 2019; Moruno-Manchon et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019), and they both increase the frequency of mtDNA deletions (Genc et al., 2014; Adachi et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Song et al., 2017; Songbo et al., 2019; Moruno-Manchon et al., 2018; and Ren et al., 2019.

claim: Doxorubicin and cisplatin both increase the frequency of mtDNA deletions.
source: Their long-term administration cause oxidative injury to a variety of cells and tissues (Song et al., 2017; Songbo et al., 2019; Moruno-Manchon et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019), and they both increase the frequency of mtDNA deletions (Genc et al., 2014; Adachi et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Genc et al., 2014 and Adachi et al., 1993.
